mechanism_narrative: The recent rebound in WORKPLACES mobility, together with a still-less-negative TRANSIT series, signals more weekday presence in Manhattan. That should lift retail and recreation visits over the next four weeks because commuting foot traffic converts into nearby discretionary spending.
failure_condition: If WORKPLACES and TRANSIT stay near current levels or improve, yet RETAIL_REC remains below its last-4-week mean over the next 28 days, the mechanism is rejected.

mechanism_narrative: When PARKS mobility stays above 40 points, outdoor leisure substitutes for indoor retail time and suppresses discretionary shopping. Because PARKS is already elevated, continued high park activity should keep RETAIL_REC lower over the next two weeks.
candidate_trigger: PARKS remains above 40 points for two consecutive weekly means
failure_condition: If PARKS stays above 40 but RETAIL_REC rises above its recent average within the next 14 days, the threshold mechanism fails.

mechanism_narrative: A joint rise in TRANSIT and WORKPLACES indicates synchronized commuting and in-person work. When both move upward together, retail activity should increase within one week through lunch, errand, and after-work purchases near employment and transit nodes.
failure_condition: If TRANSIT and WORKPLACES both rise week-on-week and RETAIL_REC does not improve in the following week, the interaction claim is falsified.

mechanism_narrative: A tightening mobility regime that pushes RESIDENTIAL above its recent level and keeps TRANSIT depressed should reduce out-of-home retail trips over the next four weeks. The retail series will fall if home-bound behavior dominates commuting recovery.
candidate_trigger: RESIDENTIAL exceeds 10 points while TRANSIT stays below -40 points
failure_condition: If RESIDENTIAL remains above 10 and TRANSIT remains below -40 but RETAIL_REC does not decline versus the prior 4-week mean, the hypothesis is rejected.

mechanism_narrative: A sustained summer-style PARKS spike raises outdoor leisure and diverts time from shopping districts, causing RETAIL_REC to soften over the next two weeks. The effect is strongest when parks usage is elevated but grocery and transit are flat.
failure_condition: If PARKS remains elevated while GROCERY_PHARM and TRANSIT stay near current levels, but RETAIL_REC does not weaken within 14 days, the seasonal diversion hypothesis fails.

mechanism_narrative: Rising GROCERY_PHARM mobility reflects a shift toward essential errands and neighborhood trips that spill over into nearby shopping. Because GROCERY_PHARM has turned positive, retail and recreation should edge higher over the next four weeks.
candidate_trigger: GROCERY_PHARM crosses above 0 points after being negative in the prior week
failure_condition: If GROCERY_PHARM stays positive for two weeks and RETAIL_REC still underperforms its last-4-week average by the end of four weeks, the hypothesis is rejected.

mechanism_narrative: When WORKPLACES rises while RESIDENTIAL falls or flattens, people spend more time away from home and complete more discretionary purchases during commutes and breaks. That combination should lift RETAIL_REC within one week.
candidate_trigger: WORKPLACES rises and RESIDENTIAL does not rise in the same week
failure_condition: If WORKPLACES increases while RESIDENTIAL is flat or lower, yet RETAIL_REC does not improve in the following week, the mechanism fails.

mechanism_narrative: A renewed transit recovery above the current deep-negative range should feed foot traffic into shopping corridors with a lag. If TRANSIT keeps moving toward less-negative values over the next month, RETAIL_REC should rise relative to the last four weeks.
candidate_trigger: TRANSIT improves by at least 5 points from its current weekly mean
failure_condition: If TRANSIT improves by 5 points or more and RETAIL_REC still does not exceed its prior 4-week mean over the next 28 days, the hypothesis is falsified.
